title: The Spirit is shared in by substance and is the Good itself
english: …not noticing that either the angels too were sanctified, as men were, which is true, since they are created; or else they stand lower than the men who have been sanctified by God and share in him.
That he is shared in by substance, which is proper to God alone.

No creature can be shared in by the rational soul in its very substance, so as to make its dwelling in the soul; to be shared in this way is proper to God alone. But the Holy Spirit is shared in by substance, as the Father and the Son are, as was said in the first book. Here too, once the Father dwells in the worthy, why would the Son and the Holy Spirit have to burst in and run in with him, if not because of the unity of the divine nature and the fullness that comes to us? Surely no one would ever choose to say that a crowd of gods, as it were, dwells in us. It is one God, since the three hypostases are one in a unity of Godhead.
That he is good, and himself gives birth to the goodness, truth, wisdom and love found in creation; and that every good giving and every perfect gift is understood to be in him.

Creation has the good because the Trinity in one Godhead, which is the Good itself, has given it a share. To have some good by participation, according to one’s own measure, ranks second to being by nature the first and unmeasured Good itself. The good found in creation is not woven together with the one creating and first-working Good, nor ranked with it. All things desire that Good; it desires nothing. This holds even though the Gospel says, “Well done, good servant” (Matthew 25:21), and, “The good man brings forth good out of the good treasure of the heart” (Luke 6:45). For it is not speaking, so to say, of the inmost good, good in the proper sense, but of the good that is joined to creation and fitting for it.

That Good abounds, and lavishes goodness on its own works, so that by it each thing that exists may be preserved and remain in the rank it was allotted. It is the one Good, the cause of all good things for all. Through it the good here below is done. It preserves everything to which it is present, just as evil, which springs from our own choice, destroys. Even those outside the Church have seen this, and say: “The wicked have this greatest good in themselves: while they try to harm others, they are the first to reap the fruit of their own wickedness.”

But the Holy Spirit, as was said before, is the very Good that lacks nothing, the good that is whole, always and toward all, and not second to the one and first Good. On this point too he has received testimonies equal to those given the Father and the Son, as was shown in the first book. So Ezra, who spoke boldly to the divine goodness because he knew that, even if one stumbles, no harm can come from that goodness, prophesied: “And you gave your good Spirit to instruct them” (Nehemiah 9:20).

Matthew and Luke also show that the Spirit is in substance the divine goodness itself, and that “every good giving and every perfect gift” (James 1:17) is understood to be in him. The one wrote, “How much more will the Father from heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matthew 7:11), and the other, “How much more will the Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13). For it is proper to a changeable substance, that is, a created one, to be made good or sanctified or made wise by another, and not to be these things itself without change.

God too, in Isaiah, shows that no one will ever receive his spiritual blessings who has not first been found full of the wisdom and understanding of the Holy Spirit, when he says, “I will put my Spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children” (Isaiah 44:3). In keeping with this Paul wrote: “For this reason,” he says, “we also, from the day we heard, have not stopped praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, walking worthily of the Lord” (Colossians 1:9-10). It is clear that by “spiritual” he means “of the divine Spirit.” He means that the endless kingdom above is understood together with the Spirit of God, and is not foreign to him, because of his close bond with the Father and the Son. And again, in the same epistle, he confirms it when he writes, “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).

Nor did this escape Peter. Defending himself to those who found fault with his meeting with Cornelius, he said: “If then God gave them the same gift, granting the Holy Spirit, as he did to us at the beginning, who was I, that I could hinder God?” (Acts 11:17). And again: “And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us…” (Acts 15:8).

title: The Spirit loves mankind and is free by nature
english: “…and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). That is, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, or, as one might put it, his unrestrained and unstinting coming upon us, is the cause of prophecy and renewal, of heavenly goods, and of seeing the beauty of divine truth. For, as the apostle holds, “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” (Galatians 5:22). That is why he writes again, “For the love of God has been poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5).

So, though the goodness of the Trinity in unity is one, many forms of goodness are born for us. In the same way, truth and righteousness and wisdom above are one. I mean the truth of which Scripture says, “You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is round about you” (Psalm 89:8), and that truth is the only-begotten God; and the wisdom of which it says, “to the only wise God” (Romans 16:27). Yet many truths and righteousnesses and wisdoms are multiplied for us from above, as it is written: “The Lord seeks out truths” (Psalm 30:24 LXX), and, “The Lord is righteous and has loved righteous deeds” (Psalm 11:7), and, “A multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world” (Wisdom of Solomon 6:24), and, “Walk with the wise and you will be wise” (Proverbs 13:20). It is clear, then, that the Spirit of God is, in his very existence, a good Spirit, a Spirit of wisdom and truth, the Spirit of the invisible and uncompounded God and Father.
That he loves mankind.

Creation is nowhere written to be a lover of mankind, for that belongs properly to the consubstantial Trinity alone. The Father loves mankind: “He is not angry with us to the end, nor wrathful for ever; he does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities,” as the hundred and third Psalm says (Psalm 103:9-10). And as Solomon says, “But you spare all things, because all things are yours, O Master, lover of souls” (Wisdom of Solomon 11:26), as has been said. For these reasons too he is called our Master and our Father, since his care is blended with his power. No title is more proper to God than Father, lover of mankind, good and holy.

The Son loves mankind. For our sake, who are the works of his holy hands, hands to be understood spiritually, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). So the apostle writes to Titus: “But when the kindness and the love for mankind of God our Saviour appeared” (Titus 3:4). Whoever gives him all that befits the only-begotten God goes away having received more than he hoped for.

The Holy Spirit of God loves mankind, as Wisdom says: “For the spirit of wisdom loves mankind, and will not acquit the righteous” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:6). He did not overlook human nature as it perished. He came of his own accord, guiding us, teaching all truth, renewing us, and bestowing the divine gifts. From the beginning he took such care of the creature made after the image that he bears this title too, as a token of his surpassing goodness. Heaven, earth and sea are great elements. Great too is the rational creation of angels and of every power above the world. But the Trinity did not choose to be named from any of these. From its goodness toward man it has the name “lover of mankind.”
That he is free by nature and not a slave; and that, as God and Lord, he sets free and makes sons.

Creation is the slave of the Master who crafted it. It does not possess freedom of itself, and it cannot give freedom either to itself or to others. For the prophecy says, “All things are your slaves” (Psalm 119:91). But the Holy Spirit is not only never written as a slave; he is also written as Master and free by nature. Wherever he is, and to those he visits, he gives the freedom he has. Only things made are brought under the yoke of slavery. What is not a slave is not a thing made, and what is not a thing made is God by nature.

The apostle is a faithful witness of this. He writes to the Corinthians in the second epistle, “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17); to Timothy, “For God did not give us a spirit of slavery, but a spirit of power and of love and of self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7); to the Romans, “For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but a spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15); and to the Galatians, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’ So you are no longer a slave, but a son” (Galatians 4:6-7). Just as we were set free by the Son when we heard, “You are no longer a slave, but free,” and, “in the freedom with which the Son set you free” (Galatians 5:1), so too, because the substance and the lordship are the same, we are set free by the Spirit, through the saying already quoted: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17).
That he commands and does not serve.
Creation, whether spiritual or perceived by the senses, serves; it does not command of itself. As is said of the angels, “mighty in strength, doing the word…” (Psalm 103:20).

title: The Spirit commands, empowers, does not lie, is truth, and knows the things of God
english: “…of his” (Psalm 103:20). But the Holy Spirit of God gives commands to prophets and apostles on his own authority, as God and Master, as may be shown in the chapters below.
That he empowers.

Creation is empowered by the all-strong and all-powerful might of God, but it does not empower. It received only the power that suffices for itself, and it has no strength to share it with its fellow slaves. But the Spirit of God empowers by his fruitful, nourishing and unfailing might, since he is Creator and not creature. For the Saviour says in the Acts, “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts 1:8), for without his coming we have no power or hope toward God.

Two further things should be noticed here. First, the Saviour shows that the Holy Spirit came with authority. Second, the Spirit did not come as his own messenger; he was announced beforehand by the great God and Saviour himself. So again he says, “But you, stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). And this was the power of the Holy Spirit.

Paul writes to the Romans words that no one can easily admire or explain as they deserve, least of all in passing: “I have, then, confidence in Christ Jesus toward God. For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has worked through me, in word and deed, to bring the Gentiles to obedience, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:17-19).
That he does not lie, which is proper to God alone.

Creation does not always speak the truth. Of its own will, as one side of its changeableness, it sometimes lies too. Among the bodiless powers the devil does; among those in the flesh, as Scripture says, “Every man is a liar” (Psalm 116:11), and, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5:6). Even those outside the Church wrote, “Father God will be no helper to liars.” And so among the saints: Paul says of the apostles, “But when I saw that they were not walking straight according to the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all” (Galatians 2:14) what he said. Truly, never to lie belongs to the divine nature alone. That is why he wrote to the Hebrews, “so that,” he says, “through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge may have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18).

But the Holy Spirit’s communion with the Father and the Son is a communion in nature, so it extends to all things, and so also to never lying. For he is the Spirit of truth of God, as was said before. He speaks by the one will of the Father and the Son and himself, and does not speak from himself, as the Son bore witness of him: “He will not speak on his own” (John 16:13).
That he is truth, because he is in full accord with the one Godhead.

Nothing in creation has been called “truth,” because the divine truth is one, just as holiness and goodness are one; and from that one source, we confess, these gifts have come to each of us. But the Holy Spirit has been called “truth,” as the Father and the Son are, since he belongs to the same one Godhead and has nothing in him split into many parts or out of accord. The Son bears witness about the Father and himself when he says, “Father, your word is truth” (John 17:17), and again, “I am the life and the truth” (John 14:6); and about the Holy Spirit, as was said before.
That no one knows the things of God except the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:11); and that, because the Spirit is equal to the Father, God in turn knows the things of the Holy Spirit.

Creation does not know the things of God. They surpass it, and no creature dares to set out after such knowledge, however highly it is esteemed. To know the things of God is altogether impossible for one who is not of God’s nature and does not have the same knowledge as God. So the Saviour taught, saying in John, “The slave does not know what his lord is doing” (John 15:15); and Peter wrote, “There are things which he now announces to you through those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12).

But that the Holy Spirit knows, as God of one substance with the Father, the apostle wrote to the Corinthians, as was said before. And again, setting forth the Spirit’s majesty and his equality with the Father, he writes a saying of equal weight: “And he who searches the hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit” (Romans 8:27). Saying something great about the Father, he said that the Father knows the mind of the Spirit. In the same way, setting forth the Holy Spirit’s communion with him in nature and will, and his equality in dignity and power, he wrote that the Spirit alone knows the things of the Father and searches his depths (1 Corinthians 2:10-11) and his unknown thoughts, which one must also…
